title: Stock arrangements, X-20 medley and band jokes
summary: DeDroit discusses imitation, pasting phrases into arrangements, the X-20 medley and some band mishaps with Benny and Freddie Newman.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. It's interesting. Well, I had a special arrangement on it.
After a while everybody was playing that same thing, so I played it with a public sending on it, you know.

Well I guess it's a compliment. Well that is a compliment. I know that imitation is a height of flattering. Maybe I unconsciously stole some things too, you know. Anything that's successful is worthwhile listening to. But I've realized that stock arrangements, every band would sound alike if you played the stock.
Sure. It's good for high school and college bands to have that.

Well I mean the first time you play it, because you don't want to rehearse for one tune. I think Peter off at the finish, he would start working in two tunes, you know. We used to say try them on the dog. I don't know why they got that expression or not. They said let's try it on the dog. And I listened to it, and then I'd take it home and I'd cut it up. And lots of times the fellas would say that sounds partly like an old stock I used to do. I said it is partly because if they had a good 16 bars on the finish and I couldn't write any better, I'd paste that 16 bars on my arrangement, you know. Sure. I used to have an arrangement called, Bonnie Rapp gave me, he gave me old truckers, called X-20. It had no title. But it consisted of a lot of good tunes. Avalon, it opened up with whispering with the drum roll. And I lost my heart in Avalon. And it was four tunes, and finished with Strutters Ball. And it was a good rhythm. And it was called X-20. And do you know the people in Biloxi used to come up and go, Johnny would you play X-20? They'd get on to everything. X-20. And I think that they used to dance all the rest of the choruses just to get the Strutters Ball. So why didn't they ask for Strutters Ball? I played more arrangement on Strutters Ball. It was a standard tune, a good tune to fit. And I used to fake after the intermissions, because you know, people are getting drunk. They don't pay too much attention. They used to let each guy play what he liked. I remember when I was talking about blowing bubbles. I had Benny Winnallet playing trumper. He's a fine fellow. He was the greatest drummer playing well. But he was reliable. He was a gentleman. He had a lot of friends. And he didn't give me any trouble. So we all, they're playing a medal in Avalon. Just call it Arton. I had Freddie Newman playing piano with me. You remember Freddie Newman used to be the dormers? He used to play with me at night. I'm good at dawn, I must have sounded asleep at half-time. So Benny says, I'm forever blowing bubbles. And Freddie Newman says, Benny, you better see a doctor. The man broke up. I'll tell you one that's funnier than this. We were playing a fake medley at college one night. And I'd call out the tunes and the piano player, he'd make modulation into the key, and I knew what each man liked. See, but I didn't like to have a lot of discussion like the man said, they have a public meeting on the man's stand. So I called out a tune and they went and I don't know what they did. And I said, for the love of might, do you know what a band went into, for the love of might? You ever hear that, Waltz? That was a Waltz.
